Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Arjun Patel, a 44-year-old chef, came to treatment years after fleeing violence as a refugee, still living as if catastrophe might break through the kitchen doors at any moment. He spoke only in fragments about what happened. He had escaped after an attack on a convoy of civilians moving toward the border, when a vehicle ahead of him was hit and the road filled with screaming, blood, and people thrown onto the ground. He remembered visible wounds with terrible clarity-the exposed flesh of a man he had tried to reach, the stunned faces, the sound of sirens arriving too late-and yet whenever he tried to tell the story fully, language failed him. He would stop, stare at the floor, and say he could not put the worst part into words. At other times he described it in a flat, detached way that frightened him almost as much, as if it had happened to somebody else; then, without warning, the numbness would break and he would be flooded with grief for those who died there while he lived. Those broken, shifting memories had hardened into convictions about himself. When the images came back, what gripped Arjun was not only horror but the certainty that he had failed. He had come to believe he would never forgive himself for not doing more on that road, that surviving when others did not said something shameful about him, and that whatever kind of man he had once been had been permanently damaged there. He did not talk about these beliefs as ideas. To him they were settled facts, proven every time the memory returned in that wordless, numb-then-grieving form. Over time, those convictions shaped how he moved through the world. Because he felt weak, guilty, and changed for the worse, he became excessively compliant whenever he sensed possible threat, trying to stay agreeable and invisible. At work, if a manager spoke sharply or a customer became demanding, he immediately softened his voice, apologized even when he had done nothing wrong, and rushed to please them. He also avoided anything that made him feel exposed. He disliked crossing open parking lots alone before dawn for his restaurant shift and would take longer routes along walls or wait for someone else to walk out with him. He kept away from police officers, security personnel, and anyone in uniform if he could, lowering his eyes and changing direction in the street. Each accommodation seemed sensible to him in the moment, but later it left him feeling humiliated and confirmed his belief that he was no longer the person he should have been. His triggers were woven tightly into daily life. In the restaurant, ambulance sirens from the avenue outside could cut through the kitchen noise and instantly pull his attention away from the stove. If dishwashers or line cooks started talking about a car wreck they had passed on the highway, he felt his body tense before he had fully registered the words. Even seeing a delivery driver with a bandaged hand or a customer with a visible wound could make his chest tighten. He had begun to dread these moments, and because he dreaded them he was scanning for them constantly: listening for sirens, noticing injuries immediately, tracking snippets of conversation about accidents. The more on guard he stayed, the more often these reminders seemed to find him. Living with that constant sense that danger might break in again made ordinary cues feel newly charged, as if the world were crowded with signals he had to read. Already braced for threat, he found that sounds, words, and images that others barely registered could abruptly become reminders of the road. With that lens on the world, reminders multiplied; he was primed to notice anything that could seem to confirm that he was the kind of man who had not done enough and could not keep anyone safe. When he was triggered, Arjun did not simply feel upset; he became intensely watchful and had difficulty concentrating on whatever was in front of him. On the line he would lose track of an order while mentally locating exits from the kitchen and back door access through the alley, unable to settle until he knew exactly how he would get out. That constant planning for escape made unfamiliar places especially hard to tolerate, and even in familiar ones he remained superalert. In turn, this vigilant state seemed to sharpen the old memory rather than keep it away. A siren, an injury, or even his own sense that danger might be nearby could bring back the road in flashes he could not narrate, followed by either chilling numbness or a heavy wave of grief. He tried to manage this by narrowing his world further. He avoided open spaces, avoided uniforms, steered away from conversations about accidents, and placated anyone who seemed potentially threatening. But keeping the whole subject pushed away meant the memory never got worked through or placed in the past; the daily effort not to think about the road seemed to leave it lying close beneath the surface, ready to break through in the same fragmented, overpowering form. But these habits kept the fear alive. Because he left the room when accident stories began, the topic remained unbearable. Because he watched uniforms so carefully, they stood out immediately. Because he was always rehearsing escape, every setting felt as if escape might be needed. And because he kept yielding to others, he read his own behavior as proof of permanent damage and moral failure, which made him even more vigilant the next time. What finally brought Arjun in was a recent evening service when an ambulance stopped outside the restaurant after a pedestrian injury nearby. A server came in describing the blood on the sidewalk, and Arjun froze at the pass, unable to focus on tickets, already mapping the exits and fighting the urge to disappear into the walk-in refrigerator. Later he sat in his car and cried with a grief he could barely explain. He said he was afraid that if this continued he would lose the only work that had given his life structure, and more than that, he was afraid he would remain forever the man who survived by doing too little. What he hoped for, quietly, was not to forget, but to be able to remember without feeling hunted by it.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly state that Arjun’s negative beliefs or appraisals themselves lead to increased triggers or reminders.
The vignette does not explicitly convey that his sense of threat causes triggers or reminders to arise or become more salient.
The vignette does not clearly state that his maladaptive strategies directly lead to the trauma memory returning.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state that Arjun’s negative beliefs or appraisals themselves lead to increased triggers or reminders.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly convey that his sense of threat causes triggers or reminders to arise or become more salient.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette does not clearly state that his maladaptive strategies directly lead to the trauma memory returning.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
